utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Please be seated. Could you please call our case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Branko Lukic with Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The OTP had a request regarding the trial next Monday. Can you please let us know what is the newest development from your point of view.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honour said you would give me an answer today. The situation, very briefly, is this: If Your Honours will agree, for the first hour and a half to the break, to have documents read, I can complete the witness-in-chief in the other Court and will come straight back here. Because I can leave cross-examination to someone else. If Your Honours won't agree to that, then we will have to stop the witness coming who's already coming, try and interpose another witness, and let the Defence know that there will be a different witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In which case? You said we have to stop the witness coming.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the witness who is due to return on Monday who is in the middle of giving his evidence-in-chief, because clearly in I can't go back to complete him at 2.00, we'll have to try and interpose another witness with the consent, obviously, with the Defence and the Judges. Your Honour, the only reason I'm asking is I understand Your Honour has been using time to read documents into the record. And as I said, I can only apologise that this situation has arisen. It's not one that we hope will ever arise again, and it's arisen out of a combination of unfortunate circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But we had the impression that the OTP knew about this problem at least since last Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Our question was why couldn't we start with this witness on Tuesday already? The witness before us now, Tuesday afternoon, we could have started, because indeed, the preference should be given that we hear an entire examination-in-chief without any break. And to a certain extent, this is also a right of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I appreciate that. As I say, it is unfortunate. But why the witness didn't start on Tuesday afternoon was the witness was still completing his statement and his review of the documents. We understood that the earlier witness was going to go the full length of Tuesday. Your Honour, all, in fact, that I'm asking is that, for the first hour and a half, Your Honours deal with documents, and the witness will then complete his evidence-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we hear the observations by the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. We have no objection to proceeding in a manner that will be convenient for the Court and for the OTP. So whichever works for all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We discussed this already this morning. We heard some slightly different commentaries now. We will come back to this point after the break. We also have to take into account that we have to go through the motion on 92 bis statements to be introduced no later than Monday, and we have to discuss whether or not, if any, there are comments as regards possible signatures and recognition or acceptance of the one or other document. And indeed, this can be done. But at any rate, no later than after the first break in any event, but I have to discuss it with my colleagues. Thank you. But let's proceed immediately with the actual witness, if there is no other observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. We will continue with your testimony being aware that you are still under the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It was a question, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I did not hear the translation of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. It was my fault, not having the microphone on. I said we will continue with your testimony. You are aware that you are still under the solemn declaration? You are prepared to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Korner: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sejmenovic, I want to just go back before I deal with what happened after the takeover to a couple of matters. First of all, had there been any change before the takeover on the 30th of April to the way that funds were being submitted to Sarajevo or anyone else? Anywhere else, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a change in financial flows. The local control of money was carried out through an institution called "Public Auditing Service" or SDK, as we referred to it. According to law, the task of this Public Auditing Service was to control all financial transactions. Therefore, each enterprise with financial transactions was to register its financial transactions with the Public Auditing Service. The money flowed from the local level towards the republic level was also controlled through the same institution, the SDK. Before the takeover, it was noticed that a number of enterprises were no longer loyal, so to speak, to the Public Auditing Service, as well as a number of banks. And they started redirecting money to different destinations. Perhaps I should also add that the Public Auditing Service was one of the disputed points concerning the distribution of power. The SDS unconditionally insisted that the SDK, the Public Auditing Service, should be under their control. The way things were done eventually, this didn't happen. After that, it was noticed that money from a number of enterprises was being directed to Bosanska Gradiska and to Banja Luka. At first we didn't understand why Bosanska Gradiska. But later on, we learned that there was an equivalent service that had been set up there, a public auditing service that was to control money transactions from Prijedor enterprises controlled by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that the SDS were insisting that the SDK should be under their control. Could you have a look, please, at a document which bears the 65 ter number 85. Perhaps we had better put the English version up on the ELMO. Thank you. After the preamble, which refers to the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there is a decision on directing the revenues of the social political communities, their funds, and other organisations and communities which states first: "The revenues of the social political communities, their funds, and other organisations and communities shall be directed to the deposit accounts in the territory of the municipality where the depositor is located. "Two, withdrawal of the revenues from the deposit accounts shall be regulated by a special decision which shall be adopted subsequently. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "Three, this decision shall come into force on the day of its adoption, and it shall be implemented from the 1st of April, 1992. "And four, the ministry of finance and the payments and auditing service shall be responsible for the implementation of this decision." It is a numbered copy. It is issued from Sarajevo on the 27th of March, 1992. And it is then signed or stamped by the president of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Momcilo Krajisnik, with apparently the accuracy of the copy confirmed and certified by the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, Mr. Pravuljac. First, Mr. Sejmenovic, do you know this gentleman, the secretary of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my copy, the name is illegible. I can only see the last four letters. This is a very bad copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This states that the revenues that we've seen in paragraph 1 were to be directed to the deposit accounts in the territory of the municipality where the depositor is located. In terms of Prijedor, what did that mean?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Prijedor or any other municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina is concerned, the revenues of social and political communities and various funds, in almost 100 per cent of the cases, were directly paid into the republican funds. The channel used to do this was the SDK through which money was channelled into the republican funds. And then after that, part of that money was, according to the needs of local communes or municipalities, further distributed. This decision only means that the flow of money to the republican level was to be interrupted, and that all payments were to be redirected into local accounts pursuant to this decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to make a check to see where this document was found. That may assist. Your Honours, may I ask that this document be admitted into evidence, if it hasn't already been, as S136.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Observations by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. We do object to the document based on relevancy as well as based on lack of signature by Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik. Also I believe, at least my reading of the stamp that's indicated on the original of the text bearing the ERN number 021164512 indicates that this is from the municipality of Bosanski Novi, so I'm not sure how this witness -- how the OTP expects to utilize a document from a different municipality than the municipality of Prijedor. That's all I have at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This document is tendered under Number S136, after deliberation amongst the Judges, the document is not admitted into evidence, and we expect the attempt of the OTP to provide a better copy. And we recall at the same time the ongoing obligation of the Office of the Prosecutor also as regards former and other documents in the future, to provide in the courtroom the best possible copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I wonder if I could ask, if Your Honours are going to or have made a provisional decision to rule against the OTP, whether we might be permitted to reply to an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I said it's provisionally tendered, and it has a provisional number S136. I don't know whether you are aware what has happened in this courtroom before. I'm sorry to say this, but in the past, we worked in an extremely good way together and heard and experienced that apparently there are better readable copies available. It is only fair for all participants and also the Judges to have the best possible document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. That I understand, and we'll certainly see if we can get a better copy. I did not understood Your Honour to say this was only a provisional ruling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I next want to deal with another matter. You told us that you had been aware of the Crisis Staff before -- or the term "Crisis Staff" before the formal announcement in Prijedor after the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any provisions -- you say you heard it from what happened in Croatia. Were you aware of any provisions in the Yugoslav federal law or in the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina that dealt with the idea or a similar idea of a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you for the moment to look at a document which is the 65 ter number 99.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which I understand, Your Honour, has already been admitted as S59.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this document is an excerpt from instructions on the work of the municipal Crisis Staffs of the Serbian people dated the 26th of April, 1992 and signed by prime minister Branko Djeric. I say signed; I'll make it absolutely clear that it's a typed signature. And I don't imagine, Mr. Sejmenovic, that before you looked at this, when you were looking at documents here, you had seen this document before. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen this document as it was being drafted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw the document as it was being drafted?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. The witness meant "while I was being proofed."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I may say, Your Honour, that would have been a real turn up for the books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was a real Freudian, wasn't it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want you to look at are the instructions that are issued here and see whether they compare with what a Municipal Assembly was to do. Item number 1 says: "In a state of war, the Crisis Staff shall assume all prerogatives and functioning of the Municipal Assemblies when they are unable to convene." Can I stop there. Had you ever heard of such a body taking over in a state of war, whether it was called a Crisis Staff or something else?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, according to the existing law, in case of imminent war danger, and pursuant to the constitution, there was a body called the National Security Council. There was an allowance for a war presidency, but certainly not for a Crisis Staff. The precise name was the National Defence Council. So the body that could be formed in case of imminent danger of war, the name of this body was the National Defence Council, and this body met if there was an imminent threat of war. But the law did not provide for any Crisis Staffs to be set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just look at Item Number 2 that says, or paragraph 2. "It consists of members each of whom has his own responsibilities, the president, deputy president, commander of the TO staff, president of the executive committee, head of the MUP, Ministry of the Interior, and members responsible for the economy, humanitarian, and medical care, information, propaganda, procurement, and food supplies, refugees, war crimes, damage, communications, coordination," et cetera. Within the Municipal Assembly, were there persons who were responsible for all of these areas of life?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were institutions for all these functions, regular institutions which, under a given set of circumstances, were supposed to carry out these tasks, both in war and in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then Item Number 3: "A Crisis Staff coordinates the functions of authorities in order to ensure the defence of the territories, the safety of the population and property, the establishment of government, and the organisation of all other areas of life and work. In doing so, the Crisis Staff provides the conditions for the municipal executive committee to exercise legal executive authority, run the economy, and other areas of life." Now, again, would the Municipal Assembly, had it been meeting, deal with the functions that are set out in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Municipal Assembly is a legislative body. Executive Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. power, the government of the municipality and the executive committee were in charge of the executive power. However, Article 2 and 3 are mutually exclusive here in this document. First, the Crisis Staff is set to distribute power, and then in Article 3, it is obvious that there is a contradiction, the way they read. The Crisis Staff, according to this decision, should inherit the functions of the assembly as a legislative body but should also take over the authority of executive power. And should have within its scope all the different spheres of life in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Crisis Staff had greater powers, on these instructions, than the Municipal Assembly would have had?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. According to this decision, and these instructions, the Crisis Staff represents the supreme level of power. The president of the Crisis Staff is superior to all the other segments and elements of the Crisis Staff, to the head of MUP, the head of the TO, the executive committee. All of them are now members of the Crisis Staff, but there is a president of the Crisis Staff, too, probably a vice-president. So this is a hierarchy within this newly established body. This could be understood as the supreme power in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we see that Item Number 4: "The command of the TO and police forces is under exclusive authority of the professional staff; and therefore, any interference regarding the command of the TO and/or the use of the police forces must be prevented." From your experience, what do you understand by the word "professional staff"?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professional staff means qualified staff, also military staff. Persons who went to a military school and who are professionals in control, command, and the carrying out of combat operations. Most of the persons in the TO were nonprofessional staff. As far as TO members were concerned, they were all amateurs, in a manner of speaking. As far as unit commanders were concerned, those were persons who were occasionally called for military drills in order to maintain a certain level of ability, should war occur. The only professional staff was in the Prijedor garrison, and there, you had professional military officers. All the other staff could be viewed as volunteers or amateurs, or staff where -- who had received occasional training only. The TO was not a professional body. They were not paid for their work. That was not their job, strictly speaking. As opposed to the army, who were professionals and were paid for what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then can we look at Item Number 5: "Ban the use of all artillery seized in combat, or acquired by other means, which can be used to destroy towns and remove it far from the confrontation line." Now, can I ask you this, Mr. Sejmenovic: At this period in 1992, what was the relationship between the political authorities and the military authorities? You've told us already a little about how the JNA was aligning itself with the SDS, but this is a decision about banning the use of artillery. How would that be enforced?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As artillery is used by the army and professional army was mobilised army, specifically in the 5th Kozara Brigade, that means an order must come for the commanders to remove artillery, weapons from the town. So there must be some local authority to tell Commander Zeljaja: "Withdraw artillery or transfer it to a different place" so that's how it reads to me and this is the only meaning it can possibly have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the army take decisions involving, for example, defence or anything to do with military manoeuvres, without involvement of the political authorities?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, according to law, the army had its own scope of activity, its training grounds, and it carried out military exercises according to their own plans and programmes. They received their orders from the Supreme Command, and then from military districts. And at the local level, from military centres, garrisons or corps. The army did not take orders from civilian structures at a lower level. The general staff was the only authority to issue orders, or the lower-ranking military command structures. The only relation of the civilian authorities to the army was to have the civilian organs recruit a number of soldiers at regular intervals, to draw up lists and send these people to military training. Another duty was that if the military should express a desire to carry out a more massive military exercise, it could forward this request to the national defence secretary or the TO, for them to secure a certain number of TO members for this drill to take place. As far as direct orders concerning military directives and weapons were concerned, civilians could never order anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they couldn't give direct orders. What was the relationship at the lower level? Let's take it at the level of Prijedor, on the municipal level, between the political and army in the period leading up to the takeover, that you could see?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The impression was clear. Most of the major problems -- concerning most of the major problems, they had the same views. Concerning mobilisation, concerning the need to fight in Croatia, concerning the holding of a referendum, the declaration of independence. The army's views, and I'm speaking about the local level now, and the views of the SDS were identical. Also at the republic level, they were identical or nearly identical as concerns all these matters. There were no major differences. Commander Arsic publicly expressed his gratitude to the SDS on several occasions for its understanding of the needs of the army and for its having assumed the role of someone who assisted the army, because the army's goal was not to protect the SDS only, but all people. So we did have an opportunity to listen to these public recognitions. There were never any discrepancies or disagreements between Arsic, Zeljaja, or the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, if we look at the next item, it states: "The work of the Crisis Staff is based on constitutional and legal provisions and on decisions reached by the assembly, presidency, and government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Seven, Crisis Staff shall convene a meeting of the Municipal Assembly as soon as circumstances permit to have its work, conclusions, and decisions verified. "Eight, the Crisis Staff has the obligation to provide working and living conditions for the JNA to ensure a fair attitude towards the JNA officers and soldiers, and prevent them from being humiliated or insulted in any way. As far as the attitude towards army property is concerned, it must be based on the obligatory consultations with the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Nine, the Crisis Staff shall provide--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. May I interrupt you. You should be aware that this document was read out in the courtroom in total before, and I'm sure the witness having the document before himself is able to read. We do not need to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd be grateful to any indications. I was following Your Honours' instruction that the whole should be read out in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It was read out on the 10th of June at 16.04, page 8, line 4 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, finally this, then: Can I just ask you about the last paragraph, which is number 14. If I can just read that: "The Crisis Staff shall convene and make decisions in the presence of all its members," et cetera, and "submit weekly reports to the regional and state organisations of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Can I just ask you this: Was the assembly, the Municipal Assembly, obliged to send weekly reports to the republican assembly, the republic level assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. There were institutions which had their superior Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. bodies at the level of the republic. And in accordance with the relevant regulations, they sent their reports. And it is possible that the police also sent their reports, financial institutions submitted theirs. But the assembly never submitted any reports to anyone. Sometimes, the situation in the assembly was reported by the deputies at the republican assembly. But as far as the institutions are concerned, the local-level institutions, they had their superiors at the level of the republic. Here, we have the Crisis Staff and the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo, and also the war presidency in Prijedor, that is the Crisis Staff in Prijedor, or in any other municipality where such a Crisis Staff was established. Because the same pattern was followed in all of these municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can take that document away now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were describing yesterday the takeover and what happened. I want you please now to look at a document, Rule 65 ter Number 104. This is a document apparently from the Prijedor public security station dated the 30th of April, 1992, being sent to the Banja Luka CSB. This appears, if one looks at the copy, to be signed by Simo Drljaca. Now, before the 30th of April, had you come across Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw him several times. I knew him by sight. I did not have any direct contact with him by virtue of my function. I did contact with Mr. Talundzic, who was the police chief, but I did not have any such contact with Mr. Simo Drljaca. But I did know him. I saw him several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the 30th of April, was he actually the chief of the public security service?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is a description, apparently, of the takeover, and I just want to see if it accords to what you saw happening. "In reference to your dispatch of the above number and date, we hereby notify you of the following: That of ten police stations with numbering 1587 members were mobilised, all callups were responded to, and there was no avoidance of work obligations. At 0400 hours, in keeping with the conclusions reached by the executive committee of the Serbian assembly of the Prijedor Municipality, power was taken over in the territory of the municipality when possession was taken of all public security stations and other strategic points. These activities were carried out in a synchronised action and not a single bullet was fired. The normal work and functioning of the service was ensured by organising security guards and patrols. Economic and noneconomic organisations are operating normally, and we should inform you in due time about our future activities." First of all, I don't imagine you can deal with the number of police that were mobilised, but would you agree with the assessment that these activities were carried out in synchronised action and not a single bullet was fired?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would. And I believe that I have explained what I had seen in my testimony yesterday. It was perfectly clear that without adequate preparations, it was not possible to deploy such a large number of people within only eight hours. The number of people that I saw on my way to work, as I travelled from my home to the municipal building and the party headquarters, nor was it possible to ensure a sufficient number of sandbags, messengers, duty officers at every important point, in every important location in the town. So there must have been very serious and long-term preparations that had taken place before that. In particular, because of the fact that the majority of the people manning the checkpoints were recognised by the locals, by the people with whom they had socialised a few days before that. So there must have been also some kind of psychological preparation for that. That could not have taken place overnight. Dozens of armed soldiers were deployed in the centre of the town only. I don't know how many there were in the overall municipality, so it is quite possible that the number was even larger. I cannot confirm or deny this number, 1587. I know that there were quite a few of them in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just two other matters on this document. It says: "The normal work and functioning of the service was ensured by organising security guards and patrols." I think you've told us about the sandbags and those, but were buildings being guarded by security guards, looked after?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They guarded the PTT building, the banks, the SDK, the main junctions in the town, the railway station, the bus station, production plans, bridges, all important locations and major intersections in the town were manned by soldiers with weapons. And some of these location were further secured with sandbags, and some even had snipers there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if this has been admitted. If not, may it be admitted -- it has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, as S137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Our only objection is limited to the signature. The witness clearly testified he only saw Mr. Drljaca on a number of occasions. He hasn't verified his signature. It's unclear to us. So, just based on that we think they laid the improper foundation and have not identified the signature as being properly that of the individual it purports to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for the comments. Nevertheless, in this case, the document, the copy, is readable, but I take the opportunity to remind the OTP on the ongoing obligation to present the original if possible, or the best readable copy for the parties. It really facilitates, as we have seen on the occasion of another example, our work here. This document under 65 ter, having the number 104, is admitted into evidence as S137A and B.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just ask on that matter, I was aware of Your Honours' request for originals. Does Your Honour want originals for every document, or just documents that are not as legible as others?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the documents admitted into evidence, especially those documents where the signature is contested or, also for us, difficult to recognise. And as I mentioned just before, on the last occasion when we got another document, it is easier for all the participants to work on this basis. I have no doubt at all that from your experience, you would hardly work on the basis of such copies. You would always use originals. It's only due to the special problems inside this Tribunal that we have first of all to work with copies. But when a document is contested, and especially when it comes to the question whether there is a signature, is it the correct signature, and then to decide whether we need, for example, expert witness on a signature, then indeed it is necessary that at least the document is once provided and make accessible for the parties and the Judges, it's a better basis for our evaluation of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll leave it for Monday's session, if I may, for Mr. Koumjian to deal with, because there are a number of problems because of the nature of this institution in giving the Court originals to keep, if you see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We don't want to keep them. It is only to be for one inspection in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, can I now move to -- you've described the takeover -- you've described the lockout from the municipal building. Between then and, and as we're going to hear about, the attacks at the end of May, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between that day and the attack at the end of May, I stayed mainly in the area of Kozarac and Trnopolje. I never went back to Prijedor Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. except on one occasion -- no, actually I visited Prijedor on two occasions during that period of time. We could no longer work at the party, at the party headquarters at least. Political work was banned, generally speaking, and our people were denied access to the municipal building and other public institutions. Ever from that first day when the officials and public servants in general were denied access to the municipal building, a number of dismissals followed. Very soon, local transport companies stopped driving to Prijedor -- to Kozarac, I'm sorry, and Trnopolje. So except for the area of Prijedor and perhaps the area of Omarska, other areas were being neglected. Shortly after the takeover, students stopped going to schools in Prijedor, stopped going to schools to Prijedor. And we were left on our own in Kozarac and Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you hear about an order being issued for mobilisation in the territory of what was then called the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. It took place at the beginning of May, I think, 1992. They issued an announcement which was broadcast over the radio and TV. It was a general mobilisation. They started mobilising the entire population, the entire Serb population in Prijedor itself and in the surrounding municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you, please, if you would to look at document bearing the 65 ter number 116.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Which provisionally is, for the record, S138.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a dispatch from the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka, dated the 4th of May, addressed to the chief all public security stations. And it is not a signed document in the original, we see. And this states: "We have received a dispatch from the government of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina in Banja Luka which we hereby forward to you in full." It comes from the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina, regional secretariat for national Defence, dated the 4th of May. And then says: "In accordance with the decision of the ministry of national defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated the 16th of April, with regard to the situation on the territory, with the aim of defending and protecting people and property, and preserving peace in the area, the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina has made the following decision: "One, full and public mobilisation on the entire territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina is hereby ordered. "Two, all military conscripts from the Autonomous Region of Krajina are to make themselves available immediately to the municipal Territorial Defence staffs, which shall, according to their evaluation and plans, be responsible for the mobilisation, formation, and deployment of units. "Three, all authorities in social communities, businesses, and other institutions shall immediately commence work according to wartime organisation. "Four, a curfew is to be introduced on the entire territory between 2200 and 0500 hours except for members of the police, the military police, and the Serbian Territorial Defence. "Five, all paramilitary formations and individuals in possession of illegal weapons and ammunition are hereby called upon immediately, and at the latest, by 1500 hours on the 11th of May, 1992, to hand over their weapons to municipal Territorial Defence staffs or the nearest public security station. Upon expiry of this deadline, the relevant authorities shall conduct searches and seize weapons and ammunition and apply the most rigorous sanctions. "Explanations" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour wish this to be read out? It's just a description of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's up to you, what you want to introduce during examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll leave that part, then. We see that that was apparently an order or decision issued by the secretary of the regional secretariat for national defence, Lieutenant-Colonel Milorad Sajic. And then added: "With regard to the above-mentioned, it is necessary that you immediately and without delay undertake the necessary activities described in the above decision and report to us about this as well as about all events of interest for the security situation in the course of tomorrow. As regards the curfew, tolerance should be practiced tonight, but tomorrow the necessary permit should be sought during the designated time period. And chiefs of the public security stations are personally responsible for the implementation of this decision."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to check, looking at the original, yes, there was handwriting on the original dated the 11th of May. And Your Honour, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you say there was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the top of the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not at the bottom of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There should be no conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, I'm told this does come from -- this was found at the Prijedor police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now first, Mr. Sejmenovic, you told us you remember the mobilisation being announced. Did a -- first of all, did any non-Serbs report for duty as a result of this order, to your knowledge, obviously?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I've already explained the context in which this date can be placed. We were already isolated in that area. So any kind of travel implied a major risk. There were people who had attempted to travel but were robbed on the way and then came back. Interrogations had already started. And when -- if we wanted to try to contact the SDS, we had to ask for guarantees that the police would let us pass through the checkpoints on the way to Prijedor. When this announcement was made, it was actually addressed to the Serb population of the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to deal with travel in a moment, because there's another document I want you to look at. The curfew that was mentioned in paragraph 4, did that take effect?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was the curfew enforced?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Prijedor or Banja Luka at the time. I mean, I didn't go to Prijedor or Banja Luka in the evening hours. But I know about the curfew because there were very often announcements made on the radio or on TV to the effect that the movement was restricted. But I personally couldn't see it for myself. As far as my area is concerned, the area where we were, every day was a curfew because after nightfall, people were afraid to leave their homes. Shooting could occur at any moment. Formally speaking, we had our Territorial Defence. We tried to organise it as soon as possible, at least in order to avert an attack. And that was -- that was the situation in which we found ourselves at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to come on to the organisation of the Territorial Defence a little later. And I think -- yes -- I want to deal with the order in respect of the disarmament after we've looked at another document.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. In connection with checking identification documents, the first day after the takeover, I was IDed on several occasions in the town itself. Practically every 150 metres, there were checkpoints and I was IDed. A couple of days later, we agreed on a meeting with the SDS, and they knew we were coming for a meeting. And yet, we were IDed several times. So that was part of observing these regulations on controlled movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour said provisionally admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have the custom, immediately, in order not to confuse, when a document is tendered, to give a provisional number, and then later to decide on the admission into evidence. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So may I ask the Defence, objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We do have an objection. Also, in addition to the lack of signatures that do not appear on the document by either of the two individuals, we also object as to relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Following the policy laid down in our guidelines in the beginning of this case and taking into account, of course, all the reservations emanating from the fact that there is no stamp and no signature, it is admitted into evidence as S138A and B.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in connection with this question of travel that you mentioned, Mr. Sejmenovic, I'd like you to look, please, at another document, which is marked, at the moment, as 65 ter number 144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Which will be then provisionally S139.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this document, can we just look at the back of it, has a signature, it would appear, and a stamp. And it comes from the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and it's dated the 11th of May, addressed to the president of the council for people's defence. "Subject: Announcing instructions. Notice on issuing travel permits. "One, all conscripts travelling outside the Autonomous Region of Krajina must have permission to travel. The permit is issued by the competent municipal secretariat for people's defence. "Two, permits may be issued to citizens who work abroad if they have a work visa, bring a photocopy of the work visa. Persons who are going for treatment, relevant documents, discharge papers from the hospital and referral for treatment outside the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Those with a work obligation travelling on work-related business [Relevant documents]." And then it states: "Notice on the implementation of the work obligation. On switching to work in a war organisation regime in companies and other organisations and communities, the following may work after submitting the appropriate documents: Those with a work obligation; conscripts who have received callup papers to their war units for one of the dates on presenting the papers; conscripts assigned to the Territorial Defence, if they have not been called to their units with confirmation from the municipal Territorial Defence staff that they are not currently engaged by the TO; members whose war posting is in the civil defence units of the local communes or the municipal units of civil defence" et cetera, et cetera. "Five, conscripts who have been declared unfit for service in the armed forces, with a permit issued by the municipal secretariat for people's defence; women workers with no war assignments, with a permit issued by the local communes." And then: "Information on taking over the duties of military obligation and mobilisation, pursuant to the conclusion of the Crisis Staff the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Dated the 11th of May, 1992. The municipal secretariats for national defence must immediately take over all duties related to military obligation and mobilisation from the military and territory organs of the JNA." Now, this document, dealing with the issuing of travel permits, seems to deal with people working abroad, those going for treatment, and those with a work obligation. What happened to people who did not fall into any of those three categories?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they tried to travel during this period, they would be returned back to Prijedor. Under accusations that Muslims were preparing for a war against Serbs so they were trying to send their families somewhere safe in order to be able to fight the Serb army. So in order to prevent this from happening, they forbade all travel. This was even in mid-May 1992, but quite certainly in the second half of May 1992. After that, there was no way to leave except when emigration agencies were set up through which you could obtain the necessary documents and pay certain sums of money in order to be permitted to leave the area. Very often, you had to leave behind a document to the effect that you were giving your property to the local authorities or the autonomous region, and that you were leaving the area of your own free will. So some people had to leave a statement like that in order to get permit to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that already -- had that started already in May of 1992? In other words, that you had to undertake that you were leaving your property to the local authorities or the autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this began as early as May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Work obligation, we saw in the earlier document that companies and organisations were to change to a war organisation regime. Those who were -- who had a work obligation, was that people of all ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In peacetime, yes, according to laws before the war, most people in their companies had their own -- got to keep their own place in wartime because then the economy must adapt to the needs of war. So in socialism, that's how it was organised. There were plans for the functioning of important companies and enterprises under war circumstances. And important professionals and important positions were organised according to the same principle. As far as this new situation is concerned, in the Autonomous Region of Krajina, the non-Serbian population was not under work obligation, except later on when they were captured, they received documents concerning their work obligation, so they had to take up their duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say "when they were captured" you mean at a later period?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was at a later stage. Some did have a work obligation, that is, after they had been captured and they were assigned their work obligation, but not at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by "captured," what do you mean? I'm sorry, it was my error.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the attack on Prijedor took place, and the attack on Kozarac, and once the military operations were through, several thousands of non-Serbs were taken to concentration camps. There were people in the camps who were assigned to certain posts, and they were told: "Now, you have work obligations." The army would then take them away to work, and then return them to the camp. So some of those people had work obligations, and maybe they could be treated according to these regulations. But this period followed military operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask then that this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We do. We object on the basis that OTP through this witness has failed to lay the proper foundation for the admittance of this document into evidence, and they have also failed and have the lack of identification of the signature on this document. And quite frankly, we think that it's irrelevant and can see, at least in part, respectfully that the OTP is trying to utilize documents that are perhaps relevant in another case, namely the Brdjanin/Talic case, which does not incorporate the issues and facts as outlined against this accused. There has been no nexus to show that this document was ever sent to Dr. Stakic or received by Dr. Stakic, and this is just an attempt to (a) broaden the allegations in the indictment against Dr. Stakic, but also to utilize evidence which apparently is not available to support any of the allegations in the indictment against Dr. Stakic. So by using documents in another region and a Crisis Staff of Banja Luka, we think that it's highly irrelevant as it relates to Dr. Stakic and this matter. So on those grounds, we object to the document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Observations in response?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in order to do, that I have to go back to the indictment, but Your Honour would prefer I didn't outside the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not in the presence of the witness. We decide on this issue after the break. Please continue for another five minutes if you so want.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you want to have the break now, we can do it. Otherwise, we could continue another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move to another document dealing with disarmament, so it may be that I can't complete that in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the trial stands adjourned until 10.55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. First of all, I have to announce Judges have revised their former decision. To that end, that on Monday, we will start with the necessary and already announced administrative matters for the first one and a half hours. And this is, first of all, with all respect due to the kind permission of the Defence counsel. But it's an absolute deadline after the break, we have to continue with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, I want to object and change it again actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So to continue, we finally had to decide whether or not to admit into evidence the former Document 144. Indeed, with numerous reservations and reluctance and taking into account, of course, it makes much sense that we have the objections on the transcript cautioning the Bench always, it is admitted into evidence as S139A and B. But discussing this issue, the Judges are of the opinion once again to recall that we have a witness before us, and not an expert witness. And we were extremely close to this threshold, to this distinction this morning. And as we all know, other rules would be applicable when the witness would act as an expert witness. Therefore, please take into account the witness has to be treated as such a witness, and not under the other rule. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm attempting -- and of course, I know Your Honours will stop me if you think that I'm going over the line -- to only ask the witness about matters he can deal with through his experience of his background in the assemblies. I was about to come to the question of the surrender of illegally -- of weapons which we looked at in one of the earlier documents. But I wonder if the witness could now be handed the document with the 65 ter number 146. And again, this document is one that comes from the Autonomous Region of Krajina. It's a decision. And I make it absolutely clear that I'm showing it to the witness to ask him about his personal experience of how this order was put into operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Already now I would once again to recall our request to provide us with a possible original -- if possible, with the original; if not, with the best readable copy because apparently here are some problems to identify who is the author of what handwriting in this B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We're making a note as we go along, and we'll take the -- get the originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, this is entitled or headed "from the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff, Banja Luka." And the date is the 11th of May. And handwritten, I think, is: "To the President of the municipality personally." And it says: "At the meeting held on the 11th of May, 1992, the Crisis Staff o the Autonomous Region of Krajina reached the following conclusions: "One, the deadline for the surrender of the illegally acquired weapons is hereby extended to 2400 hours on the 14th of May, 1992. The deadline that expired today has been extended at the request of citizens of all nationalities because of the wish to return the weapons in a peaceful way and without the intervention of the police. After expiry of the deadline, the weapons will be seized by employees of the Security Services Centre of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and the most severe sanctions shall be taken against those that disobey the proclamation of the Crisis Staff." And then: "Classes in all elementary and secondary schools must finish by the 20th of May. The organs of the Yugoslav People's Army must immediately return all records to the authorised municipal secretariats for national defence. That we hereby express our support for the work of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. All war plans and Krajina enterprises must be analysed and approved by the council for national defence of the municipality or rather the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, only persons who are absolutely loyal to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina can be placed in management positions in enterprises. All male persons fit for war between 18 and 55 years old who have fled from the territory of the autonomous region must immediately return to their municipalities and help their fellow citizens in the struggle against the enemy." And then this: "All persons who fail to respond to the above calls shall be forbidden to return to their homes in the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and all their movable and immovable property shall be confiscated." And there is a stamp on the original and a signature. And it's stated to be Radislav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the record, only this goes provisional under S140.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I want to deal with the various things that are mentioned here in this document. The surrender of what is described as "illegally acquired weapons," when did you first become aware of an order to surrender weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found out about this in the second half of May of 1992 at the last interparty meeting. We pleaded with the SDS on several occasions to have a meeting and try to figure out a solution. And after a number of refusals, the SDS finally agreed. So a meeting was held in Prijedor at the beginning of the second half of May. We were given an ultimatum at that meeting, a very short deadline to return weapons in much larger quantities than there could have been. The ultimatum was worded in such a way that it was impossible to observe it. We were requested to return several thousands of pieces within a week, or otherwise Kozarac was to be razed to the ground. And I'm here quoting Major Zeljaja, and this was confirmed by Colonel Arsic at the meeting. It was a meeting with the SDS, but Arsic and Zeljaja had the main say in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I think we better deal -- I was going to come to the meeting a little bit later, but let's deal with that in full at this stage, then. This meeting took place, you've told us, in about the second half of May.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes, around the second half of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who had asked for the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDA did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was a meeting asked to be held with whom?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Where did -- I'm sorry. Had there been earlier requests for a meeting? I'm sorry. I'll rephrase that question. Did you make more than one request for a meeting before it was held?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, almost on a daily basis. From all party levels. In the town of Prijedor and the municipal level of the party, and also at lower, local levels, certain members of the executive committee of the SDA tried to make contact with the leaders or members of the SDS leadership in order to agree to have a meeting to discuss these issues and to explain that they had no reason for fear whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the meeting that was held, where was it held?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was held in the SDS premises in Prijedor. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have any difficulty, and the other members of your party, in getting to the SDS premises?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have a number of difficulties. Mr. Simo Miskovic, who was the president of the SDS, guaranteed that we could reach Prijedor safely, that we would not be stopped by the army or the police manning the checkpoints, and that we were free to come to the SDS party building. As the premises of the SDS and the SDA were very close to one another, first we went to the SDA building, that is, our party's building, to prepare for this meeting. We tried to enter the premises, but the key to the entrance had been changed. So as we couldn't enter, we just continued on towards the SDS building. Outside the entrance to the SDS building, policemen approached us and IDed all the persons who were forming this delegation. They asked us what we were there for. Professor Music explained that a meeting with Mr. Miskovic had been agreed. After several minutes Mr. Miskovic came out and told them to let us through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask you, how many people from your side attended?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was Becir Medunjanin, Mustafa Tadic, Mr. Islam Bahonjic, Mr. Meho Tursic, Mr. Ilijaz Music and myself. I don't think there was anyone else, if memory serves me well. The people I have named were there for sure. I am certain of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got inside the SDS offices, who was there from the SDS for you to speak to?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS members I knew, there was the president, Simo Miskovic, Dusan Kurnoga, Slobodan Kuruzovic, a woman, and possibly another man I did not know well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned, when you were talking about disarmament, conversations with the military, that is Zeljaja and Arsic. Were the military there when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we first arrived in their offices, there were no military there. We wanted to start the meeting, but Miskovic refused. He said that we should wait for the arrival of Colonel Arsic and Major Zeljaja. When we said that we wanted to talk to the SDS members, they said that they were not able -- that they could not discuss these issues in the absence of Arsic and Zeljaja. That's why we waited for the two officers to arrive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said they said they could not discuss the issues in the absence of Arsic and Zeljaja. Had you made it clear in advance what issues you wanted to discuss?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that our contact person for these negotiations was Mr. Becir Medunjanin. He was the one who conveyed to us what had been discussed on a previous occasion. He told us that he had managed to ask Simo Miskovic to have a meeting, and that Miskovic agreed that we should discuss the overall situation and that we should attempt to find a solution in order to avoid conflict, so that the people could go on living normally and so that the town of Kozarac could be deblocked, so to speak, so that the people could return to work and the children to school. One objective was also to find an agreement concerning the TO in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we deal with those aspects that you just mentioned. You say so that the town of Kozarac could be deblocked. What had been happened in Kozarac in the intervening period since the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the takeover, perhaps three or four days later, vehicles could no longer travel from Kozarac to Banja Luka. They were returned before they entered the village of Omarska. After the village of Jakupovici, no passage was possible. Several vehicles had been seized and people were returned. Likewise, it was impossible to travel by bus. The bus line from Prijedor to Kozarac was no longer functional. There were people who wanted to go to Prijedor to see their relatives, but they, too, were denied passage at the checkpoint -- at the military checkpoint in or Orlovaca. Electricity was cut for the town of Kozarac. Later on, the telephone lines were also down, with the exception of just several telephone lines which were still operational. So we were completely isolated. And one of the issues on the agenda was the problem of freedom of movement, so that people could finally travel from Kozarac to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was it that Kozarac had been singled out for this blockade?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kozarac, at the time, was almost hundred per cent non-Serb. The Serbian Crisis Staff did not have authority in Kozarac. The Crisis Staff there still functioned in accordance with the BH laws. They had their headquarters there, their premises, there was a territorial organisation there which also functioned in accordance with the previous laws, and it had not been yet integrated into the system of the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the Crisis Staff there, had there been a Crisis Staff set up in Kozarac, made up of citizens from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge during the relevant times. I don't know that there was a Crisis Staff there. There was the Territorial Defence, and attempt were being made to organise the population within the existing institutions in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It may have been the way it came out. But you said that the Crisis Staff there, in Kozarac, still functioned in accordance with the BH laws according to the translation that we got. If Kozarac was cut off, who was in charge in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been a misunderstanding or misinterpretation. We, in Kozarac, still lived in the territory which functioned in accordance with the previous laws, that is, the laws existing prior to the takeover in Prijedor. We in Kozarac did not accept the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina. We did not accept the Serb police with their insignia. We had our own organs and bodies which still existed, such as the local commune, and they constituted the local government. There was the Territorial Defence and the local police in Kozarac. These were the structures of government that existed at that time. The Crisis Staff in Prijedor had isolated the area, because they did not have authority in the area of Kozarac. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that the other problem that you wanted to discuss with the SDS was the TO within Kozarac. What was the problem there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the SDS did not refer to the TO Kozarac as such. They didn't call it that way. When they talked about the TO in Kozarac, Miskovic, Zeljaja, and Arsic spoke about the Green Berets. And by that, they meant the police and the Territorial Defence in Kozarac. And they referred to these as "paramilitary formations".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that -- had they been referring to the TO in Kozarac and the police in such terms before you had the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as part of their propaganda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So let's come back to the meeting itself. You say that Miskovic refused to start without the military being there. Did the officers Arsic and Zeljaja arrive?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arsic, Zeljaja, and two other officers arrived, four all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who those two other officers were?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had never seen them before. One spoke in the Ekavian dialect, which meant that he was not from Prijedor but from Serbia proper. And he was the chief of security; at least that's how he was introduced by Colonel Arsic, chief of security service or intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For which area, which corps, did Arsic say?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Arsic just said: "This is my security man." He said that he was the officer in charge of security. He also said that he knew exactly how many pieces of weapons we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the security officer, did you see what rank he was or were you told what rank he was?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing a rank, but it is possible that he was a major. I don't remember very well, but it is possible that Arsic referred to him as his "major," major in charge of security. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other officer, was he introduced in any particular way?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other officer was not introduced. He never said a word. It Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is possible that he took the floor at one point in time, but it was of no importance and that is why I didn't remember him. He kept silent most of the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So what was actually discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arsic and Zeljaja spoke most of the time. Miskovic spoke little. As far as we, the SDA, are concerned, several of us took the floor. We tried to explain to them in various ways that there was no need for them, Zeljaja and Miskovic, to treat us that way, that we could assure them that no Serb house or Serb resident would ever come under any threat and that if they so wished, that we were prepared to establish joint patrols or joint units in whatever area they choose. But all this was to no avail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how did Arsic -- you've already mentioned the threat in relation to Kozarac. But how did Arsic and Zeljaja respond?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that they wanted to disarm the Green Berets, that they wanted all of the weapons to be surrendered. They mentioned certain figures in respect of individual areas of Prijedor where non-Serb population lived. They spoke in thousands, several thousands here, several thousands there. I think that as far as Kozarac is concerned, they mentioned the number of several thousand pieces of weapons. But it all came down to them saying that there could be no talks or negotiations any more, that we had several days to return these several thousands of pieces of weapons; otherwise that they would raze Kozarac to the ground. Mr. Medunjanin tried to reason with them, and he said that it was senseless to -- for them to make such requirements, that Zeljaja and Miskovic knew perfectly well that the population there had very little weapons. But they insisted on these several thousands of weapons and said that if these were not returned within several days, then they would attack Kozarac. They also required for the Serbian flag to be hoisted in the town of Kozarac. But the main condition of the ultimatum was to return this quantity of weapons that they requested. If their requests are not complied with, they said that Kozarac would be razed to the ground. They added that they had the strongest corps in the area, that they had aircraft, that they had missiles, and they said things to the effect: "Do you know, are you aware of what you're playing with?" What they were perfectly clear about was the fact that they were not prepared to acknowledge any return of small quantities of weapons, because they insisted on their knowledge about the exact number of the pieces of weapons that they allegedly had, that the population allegedly had. The message was perfectly clear to us. It was obvious that they were hell-bent on doing what they had planned to do, regardless of what they do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two things: You say that they mentioned the corps was one of the strongest. Which corps was that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Banja Luka corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And second, you told us what Arsic was saying. Did Miskovic say anything? I'm sorry, can I repeat that question. You told us that they mentioned that the flag flying over Kozarac, the army. Did Miskovic say anything in relation to what flag was going to fly over Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miskovic said that the weapons should be returned unconditionally, these several thousands of pieces of weapons. After that, we were supposed to fly a Serb flag over Kozarac and have a Serb police established there because they said that they could no longer hold back their extremists. Those were Miskovic's words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the threat to raze Kozarac to the ground, was that said once by them or more than once?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that meeting, before it ended, did you have an opportunity to see any documents?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What documents do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- was any document handed to anybody at that meeting which you then had an opportunity to see?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the meeting end?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting ended with the ultimatum being reiterated. At the end of the meeting, Mr. Medunjanin tried once again to reason with them. He said that they had fewer weapons than they mentioned, and he said: "If these weapons, if what we have is returned, what would happen?" And as we -- on the way back, we discussed the possibility of purchasing several thousand rifles. If we had had the means to do it, we would have done it in order to comply with their requests. But people attending this meeting were intelligent enough to realise that their requests were intentionally impossible to meet. The only thing that was perhaps possible to do was to hoist a Serbian flag over Kozarac and to let the Serbian police enter Kozarac. But there was the first condition, the surrender of weapons, which we were not able to fulfill. So Medunjanin said at the end of the meeting: "We will convey to the population your requests and the results of this meeting, and we will let them decide what to do."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during -- this is the final thing I want to ask about the meeting. During the course of that meeting, was anything brought in for Miskovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a detail which I mentioned in a previous testimony. A fax had arrived from Belgrade. I managed to see it because I got up to fetch a glass of water. And my former school colleague, Mr. Dusan Kurnoga, told me where to get the glass of water. And it was at that moment that the fax arrived. The lady who worked there showed this fax to Miskovic, and what I was able to see from, perhaps, 1 metre distance, I could tell that it was a list of medicines. He said that she should respond by saying that they needed more medicines. He crossed out some of the items and underlined others. But I was able to see what it was. The list consisted of medical supplies such as bandages, that was the first item on the list. It was the typical military medical kit that any soldier needed, the first-aid kit, which meant that they were making some military preparations. And he was asking for larger quantities than the ones specified on the list. And this is -- this was an interesting detail which I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of this meeting, what were the impressions that you took away of what was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our conclusions were as follows: They were getting ready to attack Kozarac at all costs. Had they said: "Return the weapons that you have" or "let's try to establish how many pieces you really have," if they had said "1.000 pieces or 500 pieces, those would have been realistic requests. But they spoke about 5.000 or 10.000 pieces of weapons and they knew -- they were aware of the fact that this was impossible. This particular aspect of the meeting told us that they were going to attack Kozarac anyway. Moreover, we were aware of the artillery placements all around the area, and that the barrels were facing the areas inhabited by non-Serbs. So this was the overall context of this ultimatum, and we could see no way out of the situation. We tried not to give them any pretext for such an attack. We also tried to organise ourselves in order to prevent the massacre of the population --
