utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 67, who was at home apparently, what sort of weapon did he have?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 67, MK-50, a rifle. It is also an abbreviation which means a small-calibre rifle, the weapon that I described a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally the first page of this document, just to see if there are any weapons we haven't looked at before, Number 23, he had a --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 23 on page 1, we read M-48, and TO-MZ in brackets, which means that the individual had an M-48 rifle, which is an old rifle from ^^ the Second World War. The Second World War, and the mention here in parenthesis is that it belonged to the local commune, to the Territorial Defence organisation of the local commune. This is one of the weapons that I mentioned was in the possession of the TO and the local commune before the war. Under Item 24, we read Said Sivac, and the abbreviation PAP, a semi-automatic rifle, and then in parenthesis, reserve police force, also in accordance with the situation as it was before the war. 25, again, M-48, Territorial Defence, Bosnia and Herzegovina. 26, also M-48, Territorial Defence commune, and so on and so forth. I mentioned yesterday that the majority of these weapons consisted of M-48 rifles and a smaller of semi-automatic rifles as this one here, PAP. And a very small number of automatic rifles. But this list adequately reflects the situation as it was. All of these weapons are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. listed here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, unless there's an objection, may that be admitted as Exhibit S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we have no knowledge of the language, and we have to apologise for this. In order to avoid an additional translation, could the witness please be so kind and identify also the headlines on the two other pages, or the bottom lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the heading on the second page reads as follows: "Territorial Defence, BH" and underneath, "Territorial Defence staff, Kozarac." There is a stamp which reads: "Territorial Defence Bosnia and Herzegovina, Territorial Defence staff Kozarac." It's just that the stamp uses the abbreviations STO and TO. We read the same on the third page, but not in the heading. It's on the bottom of the page: "Territorial Defence staff Kozarac," and then the stamp underneath: "Territorial Defence, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Territorial Defence staff, Kozarac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please in addition, having testified on this document, as I understand, already several times, why a distinction is made on the headings of page 1 and page 2, and page 3 have no heading at all? Only if you know, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a list consisting of numbers and names. The list extends over three pages, and the last number on page 3 is 106. It is just one and the same list of persons consisting of three pages. This is the list of persons living in the neighbourhood of Cesta, or the immediate vicinity of the neighbourhood of Cesta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As we could already read in the headline on page 2. The question was only why this different headlines on the three pages, but I understand that, for good reason, you can't give any explanation. Objections against the admission into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In light of the fact that the witness has clarified that this is a limited list from a town of Cesta in Trnopolje and not Kozarac, as initially, I think, led by the OTP, we have no objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence as S143B. The explanation to be found on the transcripts of 13th of June, page 85 following.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, if I give the impression that was Kozarac, it was quite obvious it was Trnopolje, and we are in possession as the Defence know of a huge number of other lists from other areas of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, could you look now, please, at two sample other documents that are connected with this, and just tell us what they are. I'm afraid that the copies are bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour should have them. They weren't part, again, of the 65 ter submissions. They are sort of receipt-type things, and the witness could be shown them. The originals, such as they are, in our possession are photocopies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, could you tell the Court what these particular documents are, of which these are a sample?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an invitation to the members of the Territorial Defence to respond to the general mobilisation order concerning members of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the name of the TO member is mentioned, and the individual in question is placing himself -- is making himself available to the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We have the same stamp: "Territorial Defence Bosnia and Herzegovina, Territorial Defence staff Kozarac."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause for a moment, Mr. Sejmenovic. Can you, if necessary, I hadn't quite appreciated that these copies are quite so bad. We can show you another one. Can you read so that there is a translation, although, in fact, I note we have got a rough translation which we don't think we've handed in, what does the heading say?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The heading reads as follows: "Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kozarac Territorial Defence staff." This Territorial Defence staff covered the area which comprised Trnopolje, Kamicani, and other neighbouring villages of the town of Kozarac. There is a stamp of the BH Territorial Defence and Kozarac Territorial Defence staff below the text. There is also a handwritten remark. "Nije Obavezan" which means "not obliged".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just read the printed text, if you can; if not, I'll simply hand you a -- we have one version which is somewhat better?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The typed text is quite clear. The title is "callup on general mobilisation of the Kozarac local commune addressed to the member of the BH TO, and then we have the name of the individual in question, Sakib Heganovic. Failure to respond to this call shall result -- shall entail criminal responsibility pursuant to the law of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for clarification, you read out the document bearing the name of a Mr. Heganovic. Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Opposed to this, can you identify the distinction to the other document with the name of Hodzic, where apparently before the word "Kozarac" in the first line, there is no MZ.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The heading also includes the abbreviation "Territorial Defence staff, Kozarac." And in the upper left corner, we read: "Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina" and underneath: "Territorial Defence staff in Kozarac." It's not a perfect copy, but it's still legible, at least the one that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. But my question was if you can compare the beginning of the first entire line of the two documents before us, the first -- the fourth word in the first document, Heganovic reads "MZ" and in the other document only "Kozarac." Is it correct, or is it just a problem of copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same abbreviation can be found here as well. I agree it's not fully legible, but I think it's clear enough, the abbreviation "MZ" can also be found on the other copy, the one that I have in front of me unlike the first document, the remark handwritten on the document is different. It says: "Did not want to receive the callup."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take this if we may if stages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say, we have a number different versions. They all have MZ on them. It's just that this is a terrible copy, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just make absolutely clear, in the Hodzic callup paper, the -- what has been written on that, can you just tell us again?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document here says that he refused to receive the callup paper. This text is handwritten. Above this remark, we read: "Trnopolje - Elezi" which means that the callup concerned the area of Elezi, actually the hamlet of Elezi which was part of the area of Trnopolje. But it still belonged to the Kozarac Territorial Defence staff in terms of command structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And on the Beganovic, it looks like Heganovic, but I think you said it was Beganovic, what's written?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the added text?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Not obliged" and then there is a signature probably belonging to the person who took the callup paper to this individual and who then made this remark. The words --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' remark, the words "not obliged" could be interpreted as "not a conscript." But we don't know without the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. context.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, maybe you can help. Mr. Sejmenovic, the interpretation has been given to us as either "not obliged" or "not a conscript." What do you understand that wording to mean?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be interpreted as follows: Not liable for military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these documents, were they sent out after the list that we've seen was compiled or before?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were sent out after the list had been compiled, but I don't think that it was sent to all of the individuals whose names are in the list, because there was no time for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, unless there's any other aspect you'd like me to take the witness through, may I ask that those be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the document with the name of "Heganovic," or "Beganovic," we know what it's about, is admitted as S144B. And the other one with Hodzic, S145B. Translation is not necessary due to the fact that we have the necessary references on today's, the 13th of June, transcript, page 90 and following. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you told us more or less, Mr. Sejmenovic, but how far did any organisation of the TO get before the attack took place on the Kozarac area, in the Kozarac area at the end of May?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were only able to do very few things, more specifically, the TO staff only managed to set up certain units in part. And these units were only deployed in certain places, a number of places around Kozarac, not in all places around Kozarac, and especially not in the direction of Omarska, Trnov Gaj, and the Serb areas, Petkovici, Sajaci, Petrov Gaj and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us right at the beginning of your testimony on this aspect of the case that the discussion that took place at the meeting was how to mount a defence. Was there any intention raised at that meeting or afterwards to mount an offensive against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. It was even pointless to entertain such ideas considering the weapons that we had and the tanks, Howitzers and mortars that we were up against and that surrounded us. Also, in view of the fact that our physical communication was cut off to any other area into which we could potentially evacuate the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to move now to the first of those attacks. How did the attacks begin?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attacks began after an incident that occurred in a different part of Prijedor. I was then in the Kozarac area, more specifically in Trnopolje. An incident occurred. There was shooting either in Hambarine or along the road between Prijedor and Hambarine. At the local commune building, we heard conversations by the army and the police through radio set. And soon afterwards, that part of Prijedor was shelled. We did not have any insight into what exactly was happening there, but we learned that at the same time, an ultimatum was repeated to the TO in Kozarac and that another deadline was given several hours, that a number of people were to be sent again to negotiate the surrender of weapons. But also that team failed to return from Prijedor. And we know that on the following day, so perhaps within 48 hours of the event, artillery fire started against Kozarac and its surroundings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the artillery fire began on Kozarac and its surroundings, did you or anyone else, to your knowledge, attempt to negotiate or do anything with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. Someone else did. The Kozarac TO, we had an open telephone line with the majors down there, with Zeljaja, with Miskovic, and probably also with Simo Drljaca, although I'm not sure. As far as I can remember, it was the police commander in Kozarac called Osme or Osman who talked to them. And I know that he and a number of other people went to have negotiations with them on the modalities for the weapons to be returned, to determine points at which weapons will be collected, how these weapons will be delivered. They went there, but they never came back. They were kept there, and it turned out later on that they had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When did the attack on Kozarac actually begin?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack on Kozarac began, I think, about the 24th of May. I know that it began about 11.00 a.m., and that it came from all directions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when the attack began?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Trnopolje at that time, close to the local commune building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at what stage did you become aware of the attack itself, immediately it began?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as it began, as soon as the shelling began, it was obvious that fire had been opened, and that the threats were beginning to be carried out. Kozarac is not very far from Trnopolje, perhaps 4 kilometres of air distance, up to 4 and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I think it may be at this stage that you have in front of you the map that's already been exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not the one today, Your Honour. It's the one that we exhibited earlier on. Your Honour, I'm going to be told what number it is. It hasn't been exhibited. I thought had already been exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Provisional S146. May I ask the Defence, you have this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We do. They did provide it to us, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can give the Defence temporarily another copy if they can't find theirs. And we have it now on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see there Kozarac is marked, and Trnopolje -- you're indicating.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm pointing at here, that's Kozarac and the surrounding area. This is Trnopolje and its surroundings -- with the surrounding villages belonging to the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the same time, Mr. Sejmenovic, I'm going to ask you to look at some overhead photographs, aerial photographs I should say, that were taken, in fact, last year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm told everyone has them, Your Honour, but it makes them clearer, I think. I'll read the number. The number of the first one I'm going to ask the witness to look at is 01002426. I can hand -- we have got a spare copy for the witness. Your Honour, I should add, these were taken in the year 2000, and I'm asked if I can -- I gather the photographs are all part of the same exhibit, S15. So perhaps we could make that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If the registry could assist me, the new number, the next number within the bundle of S15.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be S15-35.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you indicate, Mr. Sejmenovic, firstly the centre of the picture, what's that, the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre of the photograph where I'm pointing now, that's the Kozarac area. This is the town of Kozarac. And this is the wider Kozarac area. This is looking from the Kozara Mount. At the far right end, you can see a section of the town of Prijedor. And on the left-hand side, you can see the road to Trnopolje. What I'm pointing at now is the Trnopolje area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If -- so, can we just -- is that the road we can see running from where you indicated Prijedor along, and if you just trace it so that everybody can see the Prijedor Road.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I'm tracing it now. This is the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road. So it goes from Prijedor, and I'm tracing it now, passing through Kozarac in part, continuing on towards Omarska, and then on to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And so if you were coming from Prijedor, in order to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. get into the, as it were, the main street -- I know that's a horrible Americanism, but the main part of the town -- would you turn left at the sort of crossroads we can just make out?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you approach Kozarac this way on your way into the town, you turn left coming from Prijedor. Coming from Banja Luka, you turn right to get into Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then we can see, as you've indicated, Trnopolje over on the left -- top left of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road to Trnopolje, I'm tracing it now with the pointer. And here it reaches Trnopolje itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may be, Your Honour, it's worth looking at one more photograph. Could the witness be handed photograph number 01002428. Again, we have a spare copy if perhaps the witness can...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the record, S15-36.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- yes, if you tell us what we're looking at now.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a photograph of the same place but looking from the opposite direction. This is from the direction of Trnopolje. The photo comprises the Kozarac area, and the town of Prijedor. And the photograph we had before was taken from the opposite end. The road that I showed on the previous photograph can be seen here clearly. I'm tracing it now. And the Kozarac/Trnopolje Road can also be seen clearly. I am tracing it, and then it continues further on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, when the attack on Kozarac took place, were you able to see where the artillery was stationed?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the artillery positions had been observed earlier, as I've already mentioned. You could clearly hear them, and you could hear where artillery fire was coming from. And we had known that there were artillery positions there. That was from the direction of the quarry. It's a bit further off from where I'm pointing at now, from the direction of Benkovac, from the direction of Prijedor, that is, Urije, mortar fire from this direction I'm tracing now. So that's towards Kozarac. Also, artillery fire from the direction of Petrov Gaj and Omarska had been observed, also towards Kozarac. These were the positions observed by either myself or by other eyewitnesses who said they had seen them, they had noticed them. Perhaps there were other positions, too, but I couldn't say anything about it. Sometimes you couldn't distinguish because fire -- shells were coming from all possible directions, and all you can hear all around you was just thunder. Two shells were fired from this direction, from the direction of Ribnjak, Tomasica Hill in the direction of Kozarac. And that's where I'm pointing now, and these shells fell on Trnopolje. And neither Kozarac nor Trnopolje were shelled from this position afterwards. But we had known, since a month at least before the event took place, that there were artillery positions there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You told us that yesterday, Mr. Sejmenovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Unless Your Honours have any questions about the photographs, I'll take them away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any objections as regards the map and the two photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, the map S146. The photograph ending with number 2426 as S15-35. The one ending with 2428 as S15-36.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you told us, Mr. Sejmenovic, you were in Trnopolje, and you heard and saw the attack. What did you actually do yourself, after the attack began?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the attack began, it was a heavy attack, a very intense attack. There was chaos. Radio communications between the TO staff in Kozarac and the local staff in Trnopolje were cut off. At the same time, the Serbian radio in Prijedor reported that long military convoys were headed for Kozarac from the Prijedor direction down the Prijedor/Trnopolje Road as well as down the Prijedor/Kozara/Trnopolje/Banja Luka Road. As no one had enough fuel to use cars in the local commune, we had run out of fuel. I rode my bike to Kozarac to see what was happening and see what the results of the negotiations were. I managed to just almost reach Kozarac but stopped short, perhaps 3 or 400 metres away from it where shells were falling. That means the petrol station and the crossroads on the road to Kozarac. Everything was on fire. I stayed there for a while, thinking that the shelling may stop. I wanted to enter Kozarac, but the shelling didn't stop, so I just returned by bike to the TO staff. That's where all communication with the staff in Kozarac stopped. Later on, I found out that communications had broken down with the staff in other places, too, and that's when the whole thing began to fall apart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, had there been any warning at all, as far as you were aware, through the radio or through loud speakers, megaphones that the town was about to be shelled at that moment?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, and from what I've heard, there were some warnings that the army would be passing through there, that the weapons were to be turned in, that the Trnopolje area would be a safety zone, and that people could go there for shelter. However, as far as public announcements, warnings, are concerned, warnings by the army or the Crisis Staff through the radio, no mention was made of shelling or threats of shelling. They only talked about the extremists and about the ultimatum to the extremists to hand in their weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any opportunity given to the civilian population, that is, nonmembers of the TO, women, old men, over age, or children, that they should leave the area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were given an opportunity, that is, there was an announcement through the radio, but that was only after the shelling had stopped. And the shelling went on continually for 48 hours without interruption, two days and two nights on end. During that time, many, many civilians were killed. The Serbian army gave us no respite for civilians to be evacuated and to withdraw. Some of the civilians were evacuated, but only those living on -- in the fringe areas of the town of Kozarac. The population was evacuated in a very chaotic way. The population above Kozarac withdrew towards Trnopolje, and population was running towards Kozarac from Trnopolje in a convoy. These two convoys met halfway down the road, and I happened to be there. In that period, any sort of traffic or transport was blocked between Kozarac and Trnopolje, in either direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that when the shelling began, you got as far as the crossroads, and you could see that houses were on fire. By the time the shelling ended, were you able to see, after the 48 hours you've spoken about, what the level of destruction was?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment I reached Kozarac was about 40 minutes after the shelling had begun. The distance from which I was watching, I could only see smoke everywhere, and I could see houses falling and bursting at the seams. I could not see the full scale of destruction from my position. We could only see for ourselves after two or three days when the infantry got into Kozarac and started burning houses one by one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what -- I'm sorry. That's what I asked you. When you finally got into Kozarac, what was the level of destruction that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the shelling had stopped, which was around noon or early afternoon on the second day from the beginning of the shelling, and those who had been wounded, those who survived were evacuated. They withdrew to Trnopolje or to Kozara. But most of the population was concentrated between Trnopolje and Kozarac itself, and I can point this out for you on the map. People slept in this place that they had run to, on the fields, on tractors in case they had enough fuel to start their tractors. There were thousands of people watching the Serbian infantry enter the town from the direction of Prijedor, burning the villages of Mujkanovici and then the village of Kozarusa, and then part of Kozarac from the direction of Kozarusa. They were building house by house, so there was a huge number of houses burning, ablaze at the same time, practically along the whole road approaching Kozarac. The left-hand side on the road was burning in the length of perhaps 1 kilometre. The day after, you could see that it was all singed. It was barren. There was nothing left. Only the smoke. Many people were burned alive in their houses. Some who had managed to escape told us about who was burning the houses. Some were killed on the run; some survived and reached this refuge. And they told us that soldiers would come and throw hand grenades through the window into the houses, and in 5 to 10 minutes, the whole house would just burn down. So this was done by an infantry unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you, Mr. Sejmenovic, because I think Your Honour said you wanted to rise at 4.30 today. Just to look at the map very quickly and indicate to us the area, the map you had before, S146. If we put it on the ELMO. Where you say the people were gathering.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People gathered in this place here, excuse me. People from the fringe areas, the areas that were not being shelled intensely started out and reached this place that I'm pointing at now. People from Trnopolje started out in the same direction, but from the opposite side, believing that they would be able to reach Kozara and hide in the woods. So these two groups met in this area. Several thousand people, several thousands of people were here in the open, women, children, vehicles. The most intense shelling took place here in this part. Kozarac itself, part of Kamicani, the whole of Kozarusa, and parts of Mujkanovici. The third night, they burned the villages. The infantry walked into the village from here, and around 10.00 in the evening, they reached this part of Kozarac, so they started burning houses in this part, in the late evening hours. And from this position that I'm pointing at now, we could see the soldiers run by the houses and we could see people trying to escape because there was nothing between us, and there was heavy fire in the background. So this whole area that I'm pointing at now was burning. It was ablaze.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This concludes the 35th day of the Prosecutor's case. And it is for me to express my special thanks to the booths for the extremely hard work of this week. And we'll resume on Monday, quarter to 2.00, with the trial. And we'll hear the ongoing examination-in-chief of the witness before us on Monday no later than 3.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour said 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Quarter to 2.00. Quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I thought it was 2.15 Monday. When I said an hour and a half, I know we're not sitting until 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Wait, we have it before us so there is no uncertainty. Sorry, it was my fault. 2.15, the trial starts. And we continue with the hearing of the witness before us no later than 15.45, as you mentioned before. Right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Thank you very much, Your Honour.
